Problem solving 2. Introduction to programming 3. Emerging issues and impact of digital 4. Legislation and regulatory requirements 5. Business context 6. Data 7. Digital environments 8. Security These are assessed through the two core examinations and the Employer Set Project (ESP). Core examination one covers content areas 1 to 4, and examination two covers content areas 5 to 8. When teaching the core content there is no requirement for the content areas to be taught sequentially, and many of the topics can be combined to provide more contextualised teaching and learning activities. A number of concepts and principles are covered under different headings, and this guide will detail where this occurs. 1 Technical Qualification Assessments: Core Paper 1 Duration 2.25 hours/ Marks 100/ Weighting 30% Available November & June & (Externally Marked) Links to topic: 1. T Levels combine classroom theory, practical learning and a minimum 315 hours of industry placement with an employer. The work placement ensures students have real experience of the workplace. T Level programmes are developed in collaboration with employers so that the content meets the needs of industry and prepares students for work. T Levels provide the knowledge and experience needed to progress to highly skilled employment, an Apprenticeship or higher-level study, including university. T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development (Level 3) Version 1.0 - May 2025 3 Qualification purpose This Technical Qualification is for T Level students who are undertaking the T Level in Digital Software Development. It is intended for students who want to progress to a career in the digital sector. The purpose of the T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development (Level 3) is to ensure students have the knowledge and skills needed to progress into highly skilled employment, an Apprenticeship or higher-level study, including university, within the specialist area of digital software development. At the end of the Technical Qualification, students are expected to demonstrate threshold competence, meaning that they have gained the core knowledge and skills related to digital software development and are well placed to develop full occupational competence with additional development and support once in employment in the digital sector. Student profile and progression Students undertaking this Technical Qualification will be 16–19 years old and in full-time education. The typical student has: ● a clear idea about the industry sector in which they wish to pursue a career ● an idea of the type of job role they would like to explore as a career. This Technical Qualification aligns to the Level 3 Apprenticeship for Software Development Technicians. The qualification therefore supports progression to entry-level job opportunities in software development. Job roles could include: ● Software Development Technician ● Junior Developer ● Junior Web Developer ● Junior Application Developer ● Junior Mobile App Developer ● Junior Games Developer ● Junior Software Developer ● Junior Application Support Analyst ● Junior Programmer ● Assistant Programmer ● Automated Test Developer. Alternatively, students could progress to Level 3 Apprenticeships such as those mentioned above to develop and gain certification of full occupational competence, or they could progress to higher-level Apprenticeships such as the Level 4 Software Developer depending on their skills and/or experience. This could be: Financial Value – organisations will measure the financial value that the data can bring to the organisation such as revenue generation, cost savings and return on investment ROI.. For example, loyalty cards gather significant datasets about customer use and habits that can be used to increase revenue or to sell to other organisations. Market Value – organisations will consider what the demand is for the data within the wider market. For example, they may compare the value of their loyalty card database against their competitors or the money that they can generate from selling the data. Strategic Value – organisations will consider how useful their data is to them strategically. This could be how it can help their competitive advantage, in differentiating their market and product portfolio or enabling them to explore new opportunities. For example, they can use their loyalty card data to consider trend data or commonly bought together products to determine their stock ordering or to increase sales of specific products by putting complimentary goods on offer. Use Case Value – organisations will consider the value based on the specific uses they have for the data such as making improvements to business processes, decision making or customer experience. Like other modeling artifacts data models can be used for a variety of purposes, from high-level conceptual models to physical data models. From the point of view of an object-oriented developer data modeling is conceptually similar to class modeling. With data modeling you identify entity types whereas with class modeling you identify classes. Data attributes are assigned to entity types just as you would assign attributes and operations to classes. There are associations between entities, similar to the associations between classes – relationships, inheritance, composition, and aggregation are all applicable concepts in data modeling. Traditional data modeling is different from class modeling because it focuses solely on data – class models allow you to explore both the behavior and data aspects of your domain, with a data model you can only explore data issues. Because of this focus data modelers have a tendency to be much better at getting the data “right" than object modelers. However, some people will model database methods (stored procedures, stored functions, and triggers) when they are physical data modeling. 7 3.10 Data Models Discuss with students the three main data model types they need to know, what they are and when they are used. Steps are below Understand Your Data: Begin by thoroughly understanding your dataset, including its structure, variables, and any limitations or biases. Data Cleaning: Clean and preprocess the data to remove inconsistencies, missing values, and outliers. This ensures the existing data is reliable and ready for analysis. Data Transformation: Transform the data as needed, such as encoding categorical variables, normalizing numeric values, and creating new features to extract meaningful information. Filtering and Selection: Choose relevant subsets of the data processing for specific analyses. This can involve selecting specific rows, columns, or periods. Aggregation and Summarization: Aggregate and summarize data to extract insights. Common techniques include group-by operations, aggregating statistics, and creating summary tables or visualizations. Feature Engineering: Create new features or variables that may enhance the predictive power of your models. Feature engineering involves a deep understanding of the domain. Data Visualization: Visualize your data to identify trends, patterns, and outliers. Visualizations help in communicating findings and making informed decisions. Modelling: If your goal is predictive modelling, select appropriate algorithms and train models using the manipulated data. Ensure you use suitable evaluation metrics to assess model performance. Iteration: Data manipulation is often an iterative process. Analyse results, refine your data manipulations, and repeat the process as needed to achieve your goals. Documentation: Document all your purpose of data manipulation steps, which are critical for reproducibility and collaboration. Testing and Validation: Regularly test and validate your data manipulations and analyses to ensure consistent and reliable results. Ethical Considerations: When handling and manipulating data, consider privacy, biases, and ethical concerns. digital-software-development-content-dep: Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development T Level – Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development Guide to Content Depth Core Component Topic Structure The core content for the technical qualification has 8 topic areas: 1. Problem solving 2. Introduction to programming 3. Emerging issues 4. Legislation and regulatory requirements 5. Business context 6. Data 7. Digital environments 8. Security These are assessed through the two core examinations and the Employer Set Project (ESP). Core examination one covers content areas 1 to 4, and examination two covers content areas 5 to 8. When teaching the core content there is no requirement for the content areas to be taught sequentially, and many of the topics can be combined to provide more contextualised teaching and learning activities. A number of concepts and principles are covered under different headings, and this guide will detail where this occurs. Digital Software Development Core paper 1 Content Area 1 – Problem Solving Students need to be able to solve digital software development problems that form a complete solution or a sub-part of a solution. They also need to use problem-solving skills to analyse problems and to identify solutions that can be represented as systems, processes, relationships, organisations of data or code using Python 3.10 or later. Content area 1.1 (Computational Thinking) For 1.1.1 students will need to understand the definition of computational thinking and its purpose in solving problems. For 1.1.2 students will need to understand the situations and contexts where computational thinking is appropriate. They will need to apply their knowledge to identify when computational thinking can be used to solve a problem and be able to differentiate between problems that require computational thinking and those that do not. For 1.1.3 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of using computational thinking in problem-solving. Students will also be expected to determine the benefits and drawbacks of computational thinking within given problem scenarios, justifying their choices based on the context and requirements of the task. For 1.1.4 students will need to know different computational thinking methods that can be used to solve problems, including: • Decomposition (links with 1.1.6 to 1.1.10) • Pattern recognition (links with 1.1.11 and 1.1.12) • Abstraction (links with 1.1.13 to 1.1.16) • Algorithmic design (links with 1.2) For each computational thinking method, students will need to: • Understand its definition and purpose • Recognise where it can be used in given problems • Apply the method to given problems For 1.1.5 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of each computational thinking method listed in 1.1.4. They will be expected to identify and explain these benefits and drawbacks when solving problems. Additionally, students will need to evaluate each method within given problem scenarios, justifying their choices based on the specific context and requirements of the task. For 1.1.6 students will need to understand the purpose of decomposition and how this can be used when solving problems. For 1.1.7 students will need to understand the key tasks involved in decomposition, including: • Identifying the main features of a problem • Clearly characterising each identified feature • Breaking problems down into smaller, more manageable parts • Breaking solutions down into smaller, more manageable parts For 1.1.8 students will need to be able to apply the decomposition tasks outlined in 1.1.7 within given problem scenarios. For 1.1.9 students will need to understand different methods used to represent decomposition, including: • Block diagrams — Students will need to create diagrams using blocks to show the main components or modules of a software solution (complete or partial) and how these interact • Information flow diagrams — Students will need to illustrate how data moves through a software system or process, identifying inputs, outputs, and data transformations • Flowcharts — Students will need to produce step-by-step visual instructions of processes within a software solution, using the symbols stated in Appendix 2 of the specification to represent instructions, decisions and flow of control. Links with 1.2.2 and 1.2.3 • Code — Students will need to write Python programming code that break down a solution into manageable, reusable parts, demonstrating organisation of data and logic. Links with 1.2.2 and 1.2.5 • Written descriptions — Students will need to provide clear, structured explanations to represent how a problem or solution is broken down into smaller parts. Links with 1.2.2 and 1.2.4 Students will need to select the most appropriate representation method based on the problem context and recognise the purpose and features of each representation method. Links with 1.2.2. For 1.1.10 students will need to be able to apply the decomposition representation methods stated in 1.1.9 to clearly represent the breakdown of given problem scenarios. For 1.1.11 students will need to understand the purpose of pattern recognition and how this can be used when solving problems. For 1.1.12 students will need to apply different methods of pattern recognition in given problem scenarios by: • Identifying and interpreting trends and similarities within and across problems and processes • Recognising common features between a new problem and existing solutions • Making predictions and assumptions based on the patterns they observe For 1.1.13 students will need to understand the purpose of abstraction and how this can be used when solving problems. For 1.1.14 students will need to understand the key tasks involved in abstraction, including: • Identifying the essential information that is needed in order to solve a problem • Filtering out unnecessary or irrelevant details that are not needed to solve a problem • Hiding the internal workings or complexity that are not important to the overall solution An example of how 1.1.14 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.1.15 students will need to apply different methods of abstraction in given problem scenarios by: • Identifying the inputs required for the solution, such as the data or information needed to start the process • Defining the expected outputs and outcomes, including what results the solution should produce • Recognising elements that will vary between different uses or instances of the solution • Recognising elements that will remain constant and do not change during the process • Determining the key actions the solution must perform to achieve its objectives • Identifying repeated processes or tasks that the solution will carry out multiple times For 1.1.16 students will need to be able to apply abstraction to given problem scenarios by using the tasks outlined in 1.1.15. For 1.1.17 students will need to understand how the components of different computational thinking (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic design) relate and work together. They will need to make judgements about when and how to use each component effectively in digital software development. They will also need to determine the suitability of applying specific components or combinations of components to different problem-solving scenarios. Content area 1.2 (Algorithmic design) For 1.2.1 students will need to understand the definition of the term ‘algorithm’ and recognise its key characteristics, such as the need for precision and finiteness. They will also need to understand the purpose of algorithms in problem solving. For 1.2.2 students will need to understand that algorithms can be expressed in different formats, including flowcharts, written descriptions, and Python code. They will need to recognise and understand: • The components of flowcharts, such as terminators, processes, sub- processes, decisions, inputs/outputs, arrows, and labels, using the symbols outlined in Appendix 2 of the specification • How written descriptions use hierarchical markers to show the sequence of steps in an algorithm • That algorithms can be represented in Python code using specific Python commands as outlined in Appendix 2 of the specification For 1.2.3 to 1.2.5 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of using flowcharts, written descriptions, and Python code when writing algorithms to solve problems and in given problem scenarios. An example of how 1.2.3 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.2.6 students will need to understand that the order of an algorithm is crucial to ensure it functions correctly. They will need to know the meanings of the terms sequence, selection, and iteration, and how these concepts can be used to represent the order in which an algorithm is executed. Students will also need to know how to represent sequence, selection and iteration in the different algorithm notations stated in 1.2.2. For 1.2.7 students will need to understand what an algorithm is and its overall purpose. They will need to be able to explain how a given algorithm works step- by-step and identify the problem it is designed to solve. Additionally, students will need to analyse an algorithm to describe its intended outcome or result. For 1.2.8 students will need to understand how inputs are processed by an algorithm and be able to apply the algorithm step-by-step to given inputs in order to find the output. They will need to trace the logic of an algorithm to predict the correct output and work with different types of input data to determine the resulting output. For 1.2.9 students will need to analyse an algorithm to spot logic errors that affect its correctness or efficiency. They will also need to apply problem-solving skills to locate where an algorithm does not perform as expected. For 1.2.10 students will need to know how to make possible corrections or improvements to fix identified errors in an algorithm. For 1.2.11 students will be expected to transfer between the different algorithm notations stated in 1.2.2. They will need to be able to convert algorithms presented in one notation—such as flowcharts, written descriptions, or Python code—into another. For example, students should be able to convert a given flowchart into Python code or vice versa. For 1.2.12 students will need to understand what actions are within the context of algorithms, such as steps that perform specific tasks or operations. They will need to design algorithms that incorporate clear and logical sequences of these actions and create solutions where actions are used to manipulate data or control the flow of the algorithm. Additionally, students will need to apply problem-solving skills to develop algorithms that effectively use actions to achieve the desired outcomes. An example of how 1.2.12 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: An example of how 1.2.12 could be assessed in the Employer Set Project (Task 3) is shown here: Content area 1.3 (Strategies) For 1.3.1 students will need to understand the different approaches to solving problems, including: • Top-down • Bottom-up • Modularisation They will need to understand the purpose of each approach and when it is appropriate to use them. Students will also need to be able to explain the differences between the top- down, bottom-up, and modularisation problem-solving methods. Additionally, they should be able to apply their knowledge to identify which approach would be most suitable in given problem scenarios. An example of how 1.3.1 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.3.2 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of the different approaches given in 1.3.1. They will need to be able to compare and contrast these benefits and drawbacks effectively. Students should apply this understanding to determine which approach is most effective for specific problem contexts. For 1.3.3 students will need to understand the purpose of root cause analysis in problem-solving and know when it should be applied. They will also need to be able to explain how root cause analysis helps identify the underlying causes of problems. For 1.3.4 students will need to know and understand different approaches to root cause analysis, including: • The five whys • Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) • Event Tree Analysis (ETA) They will need to understand how each root cause analysis method works and when it is appropriate to use them. Students will also need to know the actions to take after completing root cause analysis, such as: • Logging the findings • Closing the issue • Escalating it to an appropriate manager, specialist, or external third party when necessary An example of how 1.3.4 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.3.5 students will need to know and understand each stage of the high- level problem-solving strategy: • Define the problem • Gather information • Analyse the information • Make a plan of action • Implement a solution • Review the solution They will need to understand the purpose of each stage in the problem-solving process. For 1.3.6 students will need to understand how different problems and the problem-solving strategies are interrelated. They will need to make judgements about the suitability of various problem-solving strategies for specific problems encountered in digital software development. Content Area 2 – Introduction to programming Students need to be able to analyse digital software development problems that may involve software, people, processes, and data. They need to use a variety of tools and techniques when developing a complete solution or a sub- part of a solution. Content area 2.1 (Standard Data Types) For 2.1.1 students will need to understand the definition of common data types, including • Integer • Float • String • Boolean Students will need to understand the purpose of each data type and when it is appropriate to use them in programming. Students will need to be able to identify examples of integer, float, string, and Boolean values within Python code or data. Students will need to apply their knowledge of these data types to select the correct type for variables when solving problems. This specification point contains links with Content Area 6.4 (Data Types). Content area 2.2 (Variables and Constants) For 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 students will need to understand the definition of variables and constants in programming. Students will need to understand the purpose of variables and constants as containers for storing data values. Students will need to understand when and why variables and constants are used within a program. For 2.2.3 students will need to understand the purpose of data type conversion functions in Python. Students will need to understand why data type conversion is necessary, such as to enable operations between different data types. Students will need to know the common data type conversion functions stated in Appendix 2 of the specification. For 2.2.4 students will need to understand the definition of scope in programming. Students will need to understand the role of scope in determining where variables and constants can be accessed within a program. Students will need to understand when and why scope is important in program design and debugging. For 2.2.5 students will need to understand the difference between global and local variables. Students will need to understand how global variables can be accessed throughout the entire program. Students also will need to understand how local variables are restricted to the block or function in which they are declared. An example of how 2.2.5 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 2.2.6 students will need to apply their understanding of scope by declaring and using variables with appropriate scope in their programs. Students will need to use local variables within functions or blocks to limit variable accessibility. Students will need to use global variables only when necessary and understand the implications for program behaviour. For 2.2.7 students will need to apply their knowledge by declaring variables and constants using the common data types listed in 2.1.1. Students will need to use correct Python syntax to declare and initialise variables and constants. For 2.2.8 students will need to apply their knowledge by using variables to store and manipulate data in Python programs. Students will need to use constants appropriately to represent fixed values throughout their Python code. Students will need to demonstrate the ability to update variable values and reference constants correctly in Python programs. For 2.2.9 students will need to apply data type conversion functions in Python as indicated in Appendix 2 of the specification. Students will need to use these functions to ensure data compatibility during operations or input/output handling. Content area 2.3 (Data Structures) For 2.3.1 students will need to understand the standard data structures: list, array, and dictionary. Students will need to understand the purpose of each data structure and when to use a list, an array, or a dictionary in different programming scenarios. Students will need to be able to explain the differences between lists, arrays, and dictionaries. For 2.3.2 students will need to be able to read and interpret code that uses the data stated in 2.3.1. Students will need to understand how data is stored and accessed within these data structures in code. Students will need to trace the flow of data and predict the output when data structures are manipulated in code. For 2.3.3 students will need to apply their knowledge to write Python code that correctly implements the data structures listed in 2.3.1. Students will need to create programs that store, access, and manipulate data within these structures. Students will need to select the most appropriate data structure for a given problem when developing code. For 2.3.4 students will need to identify errors related to the use of data structures in code. Students will need to use debugging techniques to locate issues in how data structures are implemented or manipulated. Students will need to correct code to ensure data structures function as intended. Students will need to test and verify that fixes resolve the problems within the data structures. Content area 2.4 (Operators) For 2.4.1 students will need to understand the purpose and function of common arithmetic operators, including addition, subtraction, division, multiplication, exponentiation, integer division and modulus. For 2.4.2 students will need to understand the purpose of relational operators, including equivalence, less than, greater than, not equal, less than or equal to and greater than or equal to. Students will need to recognise how these operators are used to compare values in programming. For 2.4.3 students will need to understand the purpose of Boolean operators (NOT, AND, OR). qualification-description-t-level-qualif: Qualification Description T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development T Levels are new qualifications that follow GCSEs and are equivalent to three A Levels. T Levels will combine classroom theory and practical learning, and are made up of the following: • Technical Qualification: the substantial component of your course. • Industry placement: of at least 315 hours (approximately 45 days) with an employer to make sure you have authentic experience of the workplace. The Technical Qualification is the main classroom-based element of the T Level. During your two-year course, you will learn the core knowledge that underpins the sector, and you will also develop occupationally specific skills that will allow you to enter skilled employment within a specific occupation. This T Level Technical Qualification has been developed in collaboration with employers, so the content meets the needs of industry and prepares you for work. It will provide the knowledge and experience needed to open the door to skilled employment, an apprenticeship or higher-level study. What is the digital industry? The digital industry is a major source of employment in the UK, with 1.46 million people working in digital companies and around 45,000 digital jobs advertised at any one time. Digital skills span all industries; almost all jobs in the UK today require employees to have a proficient level of digital literacy. The UK has positioned itself to be the ‘digital capital of Europe’ as it continues to invest billions every year in digital skills and commerce. Who is this Technical Qualification for? This Technical Qualification can only be taken as part of a T Level course and is not available as a stand-alone qualification. It is for post-16 students and is ideal if you are intending to progress directly to employment within the digital production, design and development sector in roles such as a Programmer, Web Designer, IT Business Analyst, Systems Designer, or Software Development Technician, to a digital apprenticeship or to further studies in digital. What does the Technical Qualification cover? The content is split into a core component that has been created for this T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development, and a single occupational specialism, which is: • Digital Software Development The core component provides a broad understanding of the digital industry and covers the following topics: • Problem Solving • Programming • Emerging Issues and the Impact of Digital • Legislation and Regulatory Requirements • Business Context • Data • Digital Environments • Security The core component will be assessed by two exams and an employer set project. Your occupational specialism will allow you to develop the relevant skills in preparation for your career in the digital sector. The occupational specialism is assessed by a project that is created in conjunction with employers. The content covers the following topics: Digital Software Development • Analysing a problem to define requirements and acceptance criteria aligned to user needs • Designing, implementing, and testing software • Changing, maintaining and supporting software • Creating solutions in a social and collaborative environment • Discovering, evaluating, and applying reliable sources of knowledge • Applying ethical principles and managing risks in line with legal and regulatory requirements when developing software As part of this Technical Qualification, you will also enhance your broader skills in literacy and numeracy, which will be valuable in supporting progression in other areas. In addition, you will develop transferable technical and practical skills in communication (working with colleagues, customers, and clients), research and project work, providing you with an opportunity to demonstrate your reflective practice by suggesting alternative approaches to a problem. What could this Technical Qualification lead to? Achieving this Technical Qualification will provide several progression options. These include: Skilled employment: • Digital sector roles such as Programmer, Web Designer, IT Business Analyst, Systems Designer, or Software Development Technician A Level 3 Apprenticeship in: • Software Development Technician Higher level study: • Higher Technical Qualification (HTQ). Like T Levels, HTQs are developed in consultation with employers. They are qualifications at levels 4 and 5 and prepare you for occupations at these levels.
